exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index

question.explanation:
The domain of $y = \sqrt[9]{x}$ is $ x \in (-\infty,\infty). $

Transformations do not change this interval. Therefore, the domain of $t(x)$ is $x \in \Bigl({\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\infty}} ,{\bbox[5pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\infty}}\Bigl).$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index

question.explanation:
The domain of $y = \sqrt[4]{x}$ is \[ x \ge 0. \]

To find the domain of $n(x) = -2\sqrt[4]{x-2} - 1,$ we replace $x$ with $x-2$ in the above inequality. This gives \[ {x-2} \ge 0. \]

Solving this inequality, we get

\begin{align} x-2 &\ge 0 \\[3pt] x &\ge 2 \end{align}

Therefore, the domain of $y = n(x)$ is $x \in [2, \infty).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=n(x)$ is shown below.

example.title: Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index

question.explanation:
The domain of $y = \sqrt[6]{x}$ is \[ x \ge 0. \]

To find the domain of $t(x) = -5\sqrt[6]{6x+3}-8,$ we replace $x$ with $6x+3$ in the above inequality. This gives \[ {6x+3} \ge 0. \]

Solving this inequality, we get

\begin{align} 6x+3 &\ge 0 \\[3pt] 6x &\ge -3 \\[3pt] x &\ge -\dfrac12 \end{align}

Therefore, the domain of $y = t(x)$ is $x \in \left[-\dfrac12, \infty\right)\!.$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=t(x)$ is shown below.
